1.why: Density is mass divided by volume.

2.why: Warm air expands, so its density decreases.

wrong.b: Warm air becomes lighter per volume.

3.why: Trees and wind help disperse and filter airborne particles.

_quiz_pool.question: What does ρ stand for in ρ = m ÷ V?
_quiz_pool.explanation: ρ stands for density, measuring how compact matter is.

_quiz_pool.question: What is the unit of density in SI?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Density is mass in kilograms divided by volume in cubic metres.

_quiz_pool.question: If mass doubles while volume stays the same, density…
_quiz_pool.explanation: Density is directly proportional to mass.

_quiz_pool.question: Why does warm air rise?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Warm air expands and has lower density than cooler surrounding air.

_quiz_pool.question: What does PM2.5 mean?
_quiz_pool.explanation: PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter smaller than 2.5 micrometres.

_quiz_pool.question: Which agency monitors weather and air in Indonesia?
_quiz_pool.explanation: BMKG is Indonesia's meteorological, climatological, and geophysical agency.

_quiz_pool.question: If 1,000 m³ of air has a mass of 1,200 kg, its density is…
Dense polluted air makes visibility…
_quiz_pool.explanation: Suspended particles scatter light and reduce visibility.

_quiz_pool.question: What instrument helps measure air pollutants?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Air sensors measure particulate concentrations in the atmosphere.

_quiz_pool.question: To find volume V when mass and density are known, use…
_quiz_pool.explanation: From ρ = m ÷ V, volume V equals mass m divided by density ρ.

cover.title: How dust and smoke fill the air
cover.subtitle: Jakarta's air was rated unhealthy this week. Discover how density tells us how much dust and smoke hides in every cubic metre.
cover.subject: Physics · Density
quest.2.desc: Use ρ = m ÷ V for particles
cover.fun_fact: A classroom holds about 180 kg of air but, on 10 Nov, only 7.2 mg of PM2.5.
story.title: A hazy morning in the capital
story.lead: On Tuesday morning, Jakarta's air was rated unhealthy [1]. Fine particles called PM2.5 reached 48 micrograms in every cubic metre of air [1].
story.image_caption: Jakarta’s dense city seen from Pesanggrahan (archive photo)
stat.1.label: Jakarta's air quality index at 07:00 WIB: unhealthy [1]
stat.2.label: PM2.5 (dust, smoke and soot) in each cubic metre [1]
stat.3.label: higher than the WHO yearly guideline for PM2.5 [1]
story.body_1: PM2.5 means particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres, such as dust, smoke and soot [1]. Jakarta was the fifth-worst city in Indonesia that morning [1]. Agencies such as Copernicus combine satellite data and computer models to forecast what is in the air [2].
story.body_2: The city's Environment Agency advised masks, staying indoors, closing windows and using air purifiers [1]. Fine particles cause heart and lung disease, and cleaner transport and greener cities help cut them [3].
timeline.1.text: Cool morning air traps dust and smoke close to the ground.
timeline.2.text: Sunlight warms the air, causing it to expand and rise.
timeline.3.text: Wind carries the particles away and mixes them into more air.
physics.title: Density: mass in each cubic metre
physics.body_1: Density tells us how much mass is packed into each cubic metre: ρ = m ÷ V. Clean air near sea level is about 1.2 kg/m³, so a 150 m³ classroom holds about 180 kg of air.
physics.body_2: Pollution is measured the same way, in micrograms per cubic metre. Turn the equation around, m = ρ × V, to find how much particle mass a room holds. It is tiny, yet harmful.
physics.assumptions: We assume the particles are spread evenly through the room and the reading stays the same.
table.note: Same air (48 µg/m³), bigger room, more particle mass.
graph.title: PM2.5 mass in rooms on 10 Nov
graph.1.label: Bedroom
graph.2.label: Class
graph.3.label: Hall
graph.note: A room 20 times bigger holds 20 times more particle mass: m = ρ × V.
physics.tip: Turn ρ = m ÷ V around to m = ρ × V: density times volume gives the mass in any space.

lab.title: Dust and settling test
lab.step_1: Take two clear containers and observe dust particles in light.
lab.step_2: Cover one container and leave the other open near a window.
lab.step_3: Check after 30 minutes to see settled dust.
lab.question: How did particles settle? Use density to explain air movement.
